content.html:
The neonatal neurologic exam differs fundamentally from older children. Key components include: level of consciousness, tone (active and passive), primitive reflexes (Moro, suck, grasp, rooting), cranial nerves, fontanelle assessment, and movement patterns.

Structured neonatal neuro exam:

  • Alertness: Alert and responsive vs lethargic vs obtunded vs comatose
  • Tone: Active (spontaneous posture, antigravity movements) and passive (pull-to-sit, ventral suspension, scarf sign, popliteal angle)
  • Primitive reflexes: Moro (symmetric?), suck/swallow coordination, palmar/plantar grasp, stepping, rooting
  • Cranial nerves: Pupils (III), facial movement (VII), suck/swallow (V, VII, IX, X, XII), gag (IX, X)
  • Fontanelle: Soft and flat (normal) vs bulging (↑ ICP) vs sunken (dehydration)
  • Movements: Symmetry, tremor vs seizure (tremor = stimulus-sensitive, suppressible; seizure = NOT stimulus-sensitive, NOT suppressible)

Neurologic red flags requiring urgent evaluation:

  • Seizures (any age)
  • Encephalopathy (depressed consciousness, poor feeding, abnormal tone)
  • Bulging fontanelle or rapidly increasing head circumference
  • Asymmetric tone or movements (hemiparesis suggests stroke)
  • Absent primitive reflexes (especially absent Moro — suggests severe CNS depression or upper cervical injury)
  • Apnea/bradycardia out of proportion to prematurity
  • Sunset eyes (upgaze palsy — suggests hydrocephalus)
  • High-pitched or weak cry
  • Persistent hypotonia (floppy infant — central vs peripheral causes)

Neuroimaging indications in neonates:

ModalityIndicationsStrengths
Cranial USScreening all <32 wk at 7–14d and 36–40 wk PMA; suspected IVH; hydrocephalus; ↑ HCBedside, no sedation, no radiation, repeatable. Good for IVH, hydrocephalus.
MRI brainHIE (basal ganglia/thalami and watershed injury); stroke; seizures of unknown cause; congenital malformations; meningitis complicationsGold standard for parenchymal detail. Best at 3–7 days for HIE.
Head CTAcute hemorrhage (especially when MRI not available); calcifications (TORCH); skull fractures; emergent herniationFast. Good for blood and bone. Radiation exposure limits use.
aEEG / cEEGSeizure detection, HIE monitoring, TH monitoring, encephalopathy assessmentContinuous monitoring. aEEG = bedside trend; cEEG = gold standard for seizure detection.

Key evidence informing neonatal neurology practice:

  • CoolCap, NICHD, TOBY, ICE, HELIX trials → therapeutic hypothermia for HIE
  • NEOLEV2 trial (Lancet Child Adolesc Health 2023) → phenobarbital superior to levetiracetam for neonatal seizures
  • ILAE 2023 Neonatal Seizure Classification → replaces older classification
  • AAP 2024 Clinical Report on Perinatal HIE → updated definitions and management

Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE): Brain injury from perinatal oxygen deprivation. Incidence: 1–3/1,000 live births in developed countries.

Criteria suggesting perinatal asphyxia (AAP/ACOG):

  • Umbilical cord or early postnatal arterial pH <7.00 or base deficit ≥12 mmol/L
  • 5-minute Apgar score 0–3 (with ongoing need for resuscitation)
  • Sentinel hypoxic event (cord prolapse, uterine rupture, placental abruption, shoulder dystocia)
  • Evidence of encephalopathy in the first 24 hours (altered consciousness, tone, reflexes, feeding, seizures)
  • Multisystem organ involvement (renal failure, liver dysfunction, cardiac dysfunction, DIC)
🚨 Therapeutic hypothermia must be initiated within 6 hours of birth. Every hour of delay worsens outcomes. Begin passive cooling (turn off warmer) immediately if TH is being considered, while arranging transfer if needed.

Modified Sarnat Staging for HIE:

ParameterStage 1 (Mild)Stage 2 (Moderate)Stage 3 (Severe)
ConsciousnessHyperalert, irritableLethargicComatose
ToneNormal or mildly ↑Hypotonia (marked)Flaccid
PostureMild distal flexionStrong distal flexionDecerebrate
Suck/MoroActive/exaggeratedWeak/incompleteAbsent
PupilsDilatedConstrictedUnequal, fixed, or dilated
SeizuresNoneCommon (within 24h)Frequent/status epilepticus
EEGNormalLow voltage, seizuresBurst-suppression or flat
Duration<24 hours2–14 daysWeeks to permanent
OutcomeGood (100% normal)~60–70% normal with TH~50–75% death or severe disability
ℹ️ TH eligibility: Sarnat stage 2 or 3 (moderate or severe HIE). Sarnat 1 does NOT meet criteria for TH. Staging should be performed as early as possible, ideally within the first 6 hours.

Therapeutic Hypothermia Protocol (based on NICHD/TOBY/CoolCap):

ParameterProtocol
Eligibility≥36 wk GA; <6 hours old; moderate-severe HIE (Sarnat 2–3); pH <7.00 or BD ≥16, OR pH 7.01–7.15 or BD 10–15.9 + encephalopathy or sentinel event
Target temperature33.5°C ± 0.5°C (whole-body cooling) for 72 hours
InitiationWithin 6 hours of birth (earlier is better)
MethodServo-controlled whole-body cooling blanket/mattress
RewarmingSlow rewarming: 0.5°C per hour over 6–12 hours (target 36.5°C)
Duration72 hours of cooling + 6–12 hours of rewarming = ~78–84 hours total

Monitoring during TH:

  • Continuous aEEG/cEEG (seizure detection — clinical seizures may be suppressed by hypothermia)
  • Continuous core temperature (esophageal or rectal probe)
  • Cardiorespiratory monitoring (sinus bradycardia to 80–100 bpm is expected and benign)
  • Serial blood gases, electrolytes, glucose, coagulation studies
  • Renal function (UOP, Cr, BUN — AKI common in HIE)
  • LFTs (hepatic injury common)
  • Echocardiogram if hemodynamically unstable
✓ Evidence base: Meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (n=1,214): TH reduces death or major NDI by ~25% (NNT 7–8). Greatest benefit in moderate HIE (Sarnat 2). Modest benefit in severe HIE (Sarnat 3).

Passive Cooling for Level II/Rural Hospitals:

  1. Turn off radiant warmer immediately once TH decision made
  2. Remove hat, leave infant in diaper only
  3. Target rectal temperature 33–34°C using continuous temperature monitoring
  4. If overcooling (<32°C): apply blankets incrementally, do NOT use active warming devices (risk of overshoot)
  5. Monitor for bradycardia (expected), coagulopathy, metabolic changes
  6. Arrange EMERGENT transport to TH center (Level III/IV NICU)
  7. Communicate timing: call receiving center early so they can prepare servo-controlled cooling
⚠️ Passive cooling is a BRIDGE, not definitive therapy. The goal is to achieve and maintain target temperature during transport. Avoid overcooling (<32°C) which increases complications without additional benefit.

1. Confirm eligibility: ≥36 wk, <6h old, Sarnat 2 or 3
  2. Place esophageal or rectal temperature probe
  3. Initiate servo-controlled cooling to 33.5°C ± 0.5°C
  4. Start continuous aEEG/cEEG monitoring
  5. Obtain baseline: CBC, CMP, coags, LFTs, troponin, lactate, blood gas
  6. Place IV access, Foley catheter (monitor UOP closely — AKI in ~30–50%)
  7. Maintain for 72 hours with continuous monitoring
  8. Rewarming: 0.5°C per hour to 36.5°C over 6–12 hours
  9. Watch for rebound seizures during rewarming (common — continue EEG monitoring)

Expected physiologic effects vs complications:

Expected (benign)Complication (intervene)
Sinus bradycardia (80–100 bpm)Arrhythmia (not sinus), QTc prolongation
Mild thrombocytopeniaSevere thrombocytopenia (<50K), DIC, active bleeding
↓ Metabolism (↓ drug clearance)Persistent metabolic acidosis, severe hypoglycemia
Mild sclerema (skin hardening)Severe subcutaneous fat necrosis (hypercalcemia risk weeks later)
ShiveringPersistent overcooling (<32°C)
⚠️ Subcutaneous fat necrosis: Firm, erythematous nodules appearing during or after TH. Monitor calcium for weeks — can cause life-threatening hypercalcemia (from granulomatous 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production).

MRI Timing:

  • Best timing: day 3–7 of life (after rewarming). Earlier MRI may underestimate injury; later MRI may show pseudonormalization.
  • DWI (diffusion-weighted imaging): Most sensitive for acute ischemic injury. Peaks at day 3–5.
  • Patterns of injury on MRI:
    — Basal ganglia/thalami + PLIC: Acute profound asphyxia (sentinel event). Associated with dyskinetic CP, feeding/swallowing difficulties.
    — Watershed (border zone): Partial prolonged asphyxia. Associated with cognitive impairment, quadriparetic CP.
    — Total/near-total: Severe prolonged asphyxia. Worst prognosis.
  • MRS (spectroscopy): Elevated lactate/NAA ratio in basal ganglia is one of the most accurate early predictors of adverse outcome.

Best predictors of outcome after HIE + TH:

ToolTimingPrognostic Value
MRI (DWI + conventional)Day 3–7Strongest single predictor. BG/thalami + PLIC signal loss → high risk CP/death.
MR SpectroscopyDay 3–7Lac/NAA ratio >0.3 in BG = high specificity for adverse outcome.
EEG background24–48h post-rewarmingPersistent burst-suppression or flat EEG = poor prognosis. Recovery of normal EEG = favorable.
Neurologic exam at dischargePre-dischargePersistent encephalopathy, absent suck, persistent hypotonia = high risk NDI.
Sarnat stageEvolvingStage 3 persisting beyond 72h = high mortality/severe disability.

Family counseling framework:

  • Wait for MRI and post-rewarming exam before definitive prognostication
  • Avoid early pessimistic predictions in the first 24–48h (the brain is still evolving)
  • Use multiple modalities (MRI + EEG + clinical exam) — no single test is 100% predictive
  • Moderate HIE with TH: ~60–70% will have normal or mildly impaired outcomes
  • Severe HIE: early goals-of-care discussion appropriate if multiple indicators predict poor outcome
  • All HIE survivors need long-term neurodevelopmental follow-up (minimum 2 years, preferably to school age)

Neonatal seizures are the most common neurologic emergency in newborns. Incidence: 1–5/1,000 live births (higher in preterm). Most are SUBCLINICAL — only detected on EEG. Clinical seizures in neonates look different from older children.

Clinical seizure types (neonatal):

  • Subtle: Most common. Eye deviation, lip smacking, cycling movements, apnea. Often missed without EEG.
  • Clonic: Rhythmic jerking, focal or multifocal. Most likely to have EEG correlate.
  • Tonic: Sustained posturing (extension or flexion). Often brainstem origin. Less likely to have EEG correlate.
  • Myoclonic: Brief, shock-like jerks. Focal or generalized.
⚠️ Tremor vs seizure: Tremor = equal amplitude oscillations, stimulus-sensitive, suppressible by holding the limb. Seizure = NOT stimulus-sensitive, NOT suppressible, often with autonomic changes. Use EEG if in doubt.

ILAE 2023 Neonatal Seizure Classification:

  • Classifies by: (1) electrographic vs clinical, (2) motor manifestation type, (3) autonomic features
  • Emphasizes that ONLY electrographic seizures (EEG-confirmed) should be treated with ASMs
  • Clinical events without EEG correlate may represent brainstem release phenomena, NOT true epileptic seizures
  • Neonatal seizures are almost always FOCAL (even if they appear generalized clinically)
  • Status epilepticus = continuous seizure or recurrent seizures for >50% of a 1-hour recording

Seizure Etiology Workup:

  1. Blood glucose (STAT — hypoglycemia is most treatable cause)
  2. Electrolytes: Na, Ca, Mg, phosphorus (hyponatremia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia)
  3. Blood gas (acidosis, hyperammonemia)
  4. Sepsis workup: CBC, CRP, blood culture, LP (meningitis causes seizures)
  5. CSF: Cell count, protein, glucose, culture, HSV PCR, amino acids, neurotransmitters
  6. Cranial US (bedside, rapid — hemorrhage, hydrocephalus)
  7. MRI brain (when stable — stroke, HIE pattern, malformations)
  8. EEG / aEEG (continuous monitoring — most neonatal seizures are subclinical)
  9. Metabolic: Ammonia, lactate, pyruvate, amino acids, urine organic acids (if recurrent seizures without etiology)
  10. Pyridoxine trial (100 mg IV with EEG monitoring — pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy if seizures stop immediately)
Etiology% of CasesKey Lab/Imaging
HIE~40–50%History, exam, MRI (BG/thalami pattern)
Intracranial hemorrhage~15%Cranial US, CT/MRI (IVH, SDH, SAH)
Ischemic stroke~10%MRI DWI (MCA territory most common)
Infection (meningitis/encephalitis)~10%CSF pleocytosis, culture, HSV PCR
Metabolic~5–10%Glucose, Ca, Mg, Na, ammonia, IEM workup
Congenital malformation~5%MRI (cortical dysplasia, lissencephaly)
Genetic epilepsy~5%Epilepsy gene panel; consider SCN2A, KCNQ2

Seizure Treatment Algorithm:

  1. Correct reversible causes FIRST: D10W 2 mL/kg for hypoglycemia, calcium gluconate 10% for hypocalcemia, magnesium sulfate for hypomagnesemia
  2. FIRST-LINE: Phenobarbital 20 mg/kg IV (infuse over 15–20 min). Seizure cessation: ~60–80% (NEOLEV2 trial confirmed superiority over levetiracetam).
  3. If seizures continue: Additional phenobarbital 10 mg/kg × 1–2 doses (max total 40 mg/kg)
  4. SECOND-LINE (if phenobarbital fails): Levetiracetam 40–60 mg/kg IV, OR phenytoin/fosphenytoin 20 mg PE/kg IV
  5. THIRD-LINE (refractory): Midazolam continuous infusion (0.05–0.15 mg/kg/hr) or lidocaine infusion (2 mg/kg/hr, NOT with phenytoin — cardiac risk)
  6. Consider pyridoxine trial: 100 mg IV while on EEG if no etiology found and seizures persist
✓ NEOLEV2 Trial (Lancet Child Adolesc Health 2023): Phenobarbital was superior to levetiracetam for neonatal seizure cessation (80% vs 28%, p<0.001). Phenobarbital remains first-line. Levetiracetam should be second-line or used in specific situations (hepatic dysfunction, concern for sedation).

ParameterProtocol
Loading dose20 mg/kg IV over 15–20 min
Additional loading10 mg/kg IV × 1–2 if seizures persist (max 40 mg/kg total)
Maintenance3–5 mg/kg/day divided q12–24h (start 12–24h after load)
Therapeutic level20–40 µg/mL
RouteIV preferred for loading; PO for maintenance once tolerating feeds

• Continuous EEG/aEEG to assess seizure burden and treatment response
  • Monitor respiratory status (phenobarbital causes respiratory depression — have PPV/intubation equipment ready)
  • Monitor blood pressure (hypotension possible)
  • Trough levels at 48–72h, then weekly
  • LFTs if prolonged therapy

When to discontinue ASMs:

  • If seizures were due to acute provoked cause (HIE, metabolic) and resolved: discontinue before discharge in most cases
  • AAP/WHO guidance supports early discontinuation of phenobarbital if seizures have resolved and EEG is normalized
  • Wean gradually (10–20% every 3–5 days) while monitoring EEG
  • Prolonged therapy only if: ongoing seizures, epilepsy syndrome identified, structural malformation with high recurrence risk
✓ Trend is toward EARLIER discontinuation. Most neonatal seizures from acute causes do not recur. Prolonged phenobarbital exposure may have adverse effects on the developing brain.

node.label: Refractory Seizure Protocol
node.description: Midazolam gtt or lidocaine · Pyridoxine trial

content.html:
If phenobarbital fails (total 40 mg/kg):

AgentDoseNotes
Levetiracetam40–60 mg/kg IVNEOLEV2: only 28% efficacy as first-line; may be better as second-line after phenobarbital
Fosphenytoin20 mg PE/kg IVGood for focal seizures. Cardiac monitoring required. Do NOT use with lidocaine.
MidazolamLoad 0.05–0.15 mg/kg, then 0.05–0.4 mg/kg/hrContinuous infusion for refractory status. Risk: respiratory depression, hypotension.
Lidocaine2 mg/kg/hr IV × 4h then taperDO NOT use with fosphenytoin (cardiac toxicity). Contraindicated with congenital heart disease.

Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) Trial:

  • Give pyridoxine 100 mg IV while monitoring EEG
  • In pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (ALDH7A1 mutation), seizures stop within minutes
  • If positive response: continue pyridoxine 30 mg/kg/day divided BID
  • If no response to pyridoxine: try pyridoxal-5-phosphate (PLP) 30 mg/kg/day (PNPO deficiency)
  • Consider folinic acid trial (cerebral folate deficiency)
  • These treatable metabolic epilepsies are rare but MUST be considered when seizures have no identified cause and are refractory to standard ASMs
🔬 Always consider inborn errors of metabolism in unexplained refractory neonatal seizures. Send: plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, CSF amino acids/neurotransmitters, ALDH7A1 gene testing.

node.label: Intraventricular Hemorrhage
node.description: Preterm · Cranial US screening · Papile grading

content.html:
IVH originates from the germinal matrix (highly vascular, fragile structure in the subependymal region) in preterm infants. Incidence: ~25–30% of VLBW (<1500g); up to 40–50% of ELBW (<1000g). Most occurs within the first 72 hours of life.

Risk factors: Prematurity (strongest), absence of antenatal steroids, vaginal delivery, low Apgar scores, fluctuating cerebral blood flow, pneumothorax, coagulopathy, rapid volume expansion, hypercarbia.

GradeDescriptionIncidencePrognosis
IGerminal matrix hemorrhage only (subependymal)Most commonExcellent; resolves spontaneously
IIIVH without ventricular dilation (<50% ventricle filled)CommonGenerally favorable
IIIIVH WITH acute ventricular dilation (>50% filled)Less commonSignificant risk of hydrocephalus (50–80%) and NDI
IV (PVHI)Periventricular hemorrhagic infarctionLeast commonHigh risk of CP and NDI (40–80%)
ℹ️ "Grade IV" is now more accurately termed PVHI (periventricular hemorrhagic infarction) — it represents venous infarction from obstruction of medullary veins by the IVH, NOT simply extension of the hemorrhage into parenchyma.

Cranial US Screening Schedule (AAP/AIUM):

  1. All infants <32 weeks GA: First cranial US at 7–14 days of life
  2. Repeat at 36–40 weeks PMA (evaluate for PVL/periventricular white matter injury)
  3. Earlier US if: Acute neurologic deterioration, unexplained anemia/dropping Hct, seizures, bulging fontanelle
  4. Consider serial US weekly in ELBW during first 4–6 weeks if IVH detected
  5. Follow-up US if progressive ventriculomegaly suspected (measure ventricular index)

Management by grade:

GradeManagementFollow-up
I–IISupportive. Avoid BP fluctuations, correct coagulopathy, gentle handling.Repeat US at 36–40 wk PMA. Usually resolves.
IIISerial US weekly for ventricular size. Monitor HC. Watch for post-hemorrhagic hydrocephalus (PHH).Neurosurgery consult if progressive ventriculomegaly. May need reservoir/VP shunt.
PVHISame as Grade III + evaluate for porencephalic cyst development. Higher risk of surgical intervention.MRI before discharge. Long-term neuro/developmental follow-up. High risk of contralateral hemiplegia.

Post-Hemorrhagic Hydrocephalus (PHH):

  • Occurs in ~30% of Grade III and ~50–80% of PVHI
  • Serial cranial US measuring ventricular index (VI) and anterior horn width (AHW)
  • Intervention thresholds: VI > p97 + 4mm OR AHW > 10mm OR clinical signs (↑ HC, splayed sutures, bulging fontanelle, apnea)
  • Options: temporary measures (ventricular reservoir, subgaleal shunt, DRIFT) → definitive VP shunt when infant is bigger/stable

Neonatal stroke: focal disruption of cerebral blood flow. Incidence: ~1/2,300–4,000 live births. Most common vascular event in term neonates.

TypeDescriptionFrequency
NAIS (Neonatal Arterial Ischemic Stroke)Thromboembolism in cerebral artery (MCA territory ~80%)Most common
CSVT (Cerebral Sinovenous Thrombosis)Thrombosis of dural sinuses or cerebral veinsLess common
Hemorrhagic strokeIntracerebral hemorrhage in term infantLeast common

Clinical presentation:

  • Focal seizures: Most common presenting sign (~80%). Often clonic seizures of one limb or hemibody.
  • Asymmetric tone: Hemiparesis — decreased spontaneous movement of one side
  • Encephalopathy: Lethargy, poor feeding (less common than seizures)
  • Many neonatal strokes are clinically silent — discovered incidentally on neuroimaging or when child develops handedness preference/hemiplegia at 4–6 months

Risk factors: cardiac disease (PFO, CHD), prothrombotic disorders, infection, perinatal asphyxia, dehydration, maternal preeclampsia, cocaine exposure. BUT in ~50%, no risk factor identified.

1. MRI with DWI — gold standard. DWI shows acute ischemia within hours. MCA territory involvement in ~80%.
  2. MRA/MRV — evaluate vessel occlusion (arterial or venous)
  3. Echocardiogram — rule out cardiac source of embolism (PFO, vegetation, structural CHD)
  4. Prothrombotic workup (timing controversial — some defer to 3–6 months):
    Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, protein C/S, antithrombin III, homocysteine, lipoprotein(a), antiphospholipid antibodies
  5. Infection workup — blood culture, CRP (infection is a risk factor for thrombosis)

Management:

  • Seizure treatment: Phenobarbital per standard neonatal seizure protocol
  • Anticoagulation: NOT routinely recommended for NAIS (AHA/ASA 2019). Consider for CSVT if propagating clot or no hemorrhagic transformation (LMWH enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg SC q12h with anti-Xa monitoring).
  • Aspirin: Some centers use low-dose aspirin (1–5 mg/kg/day) for recurrent stroke or cardiac source; evidence limited in neonates.
  • Supportive: Maintain normal glucose, temperature, hydration, blood pressure
  • Follow-up: Repeat MRI at 4–6 weeks. Neurodevelopmental monitoring. ~30–50% develop hemiparetic CP; ~30% develop epilepsy.

The floppy infant: Hypotonia is a clinical sign, not a diagnosis. The critical first step is determining whether the cause is central (brain/spinal cord) or peripheral (anterior horn cell, nerve, NMJ, muscle).

FeatureCentral HypotoniaPeripheral Hypotonia
ConsciousnessOften altered (lethargic/encephalopathic)Alert ("bright-eyed floppy baby")
Deep tendon reflexesNormal or increasedDecreased or absent
WeaknessLess prominent; antigravity movements may be preservedProminent weakness; poor antigravity movement
SeizuresMay be presentAbsent
FasciculationsAbsentPresent (tongue fasciculations → SMA)
FistingCortical thumb/persistent fistingOpen, relaxed hands

CategoryExamples
Central — brainHIE, chromosomal (T21, Prader-Willi), brain malformation, metabolic (Zellweger, Pompe), infection
Central — spinalSpinal cord injury (birth trauma), spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) with upper motor neuron features
Peripheral — anterior hornSMA Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann) — #1 genetic cause of infant death
Peripheral — nerveCongenital neuropathies (Charcot-Marie-Tooth, congenital hypomyelinating)
Peripheral — NMJCongenital myasthenic syndromes, transient neonatal myasthenia (maternal MG)
Peripheral — muscleCongenital myotonic dystrophy, congenital myopathies (nemaline, centronuclear), congenital muscular dystrophies

1. Determine central vs peripheral (see table above)
  2. If central: MRI brain, chromosomal microarray, metabolic workup (ammonia, lactate, amino acids, organic acids, very long chain fatty acids for Zellweger), methylation studies (Prader-Willi)
  3. If peripheral: CK level (elevated in muscular dystrophy/myopathy), SMN1 gene testing (SMA — MOST IMPORTANT; now on newborn screening), EMG/NCV (rarely done in neonates; consider if diagnosis unclear), genetic testing panels
  4. Newborn screening results: SMA is on the RUSP — check results early
  5. If congenital myotonic dystrophy suspected: Examine the MOTHER (myotonia, grip difficulty, facial weakness — disease is maternally transmitted; CTG repeat expansion)

SMA Type 1 (Werdnig-Hoffmann):

  • Most common genetic cause of infant death (before gene therapy era)
  • SMN1 gene homozygous deletion (AR inheritance)
  • Presents: severe hypotonia, absent DTRs, tongue fasciculations, bell-shaped chest, paradoxical breathing, alert face ("bright-eyed")
  • URGENCY: Gene therapy (onasemnogene — Zolgensma) is most effective when given EARLY (before symptom onset). FDA approved for <2 years. Newborn screening allows pre-symptomatic treatment.
🚨 SMA is a NEUROLOGY EMERGENCY when identified on newborn screening. Pre-symptomatic treatment with gene therapy (Zolgensma) or nusinersen dramatically improves outcomes. Refer to pediatric neurology IMMEDIATELY when SMA NBS is positive.

Congenital Myotonic Dystrophy (DM1):

  • Maternal transmission (CTG repeat expansion in DMPK gene; anticipation — gets worse each generation)
  • Presents: polyhydramnios → severe hypotonia, respiratory failure, feeding difficulties, facial diplegia ("tented upper lip"), club feet
  • Diagnosis: examine the MOTHER + genetic testing (CTG repeat >1000 in congenital form)
  • Mortality: ~25% in severe neonatal form; survivors improve but develop adult DM1 features

Neonatal Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome (NOWS) — previously called Neonatal Abstinence Syndrome (NAS). Affects ~60–80% of opioid-exposed neonates. Onset: 24–72 hours after birth (longer with methadone/buprenorphine — up to 5–7 days).

Signs:

  • CNS irritability: High-pitched cry, tremors, jitteriness, increased wakefulness, seizures (rare, <5%)
  • GI dysfunction: Poor feeding, uncoordinated suck, vomiting, diarrhea, weight loss
  • Autonomic: Sneezing, yawning, sweating, temperature instability, mottling

Eat-Sleep-Console (ESC) Approach — replacing Finnegan scoring:

ESC focuses on functional assessment rather than symptom scoring. Three simple questions:

QuestionAdequateInadequate
EAT: Is the infant eating well?Coordinated suck, taking ≥1 oz per feed, gaining weightUncoordinated suck, poor intake, weight loss
SLEEP: Can the infant sleep ≥1 hour undisturbed?Sleeps ≥1 hour after feedingCannot sleep ≥1 hour despite swaddling/soothing
CONSOLE: Can the infant be consoled within 10 min?Settles with swaddling, rocking, skin-to-skinInconsolable for >10 min despite all non-pharm interventions

If ALL three are adequate → continue non-pharmacologic care.
If ANY ONE is inadequate despite optimized non-pharmacologic care → consider pharmacotherapy.

✓ ESC has reduced pharmacotherapy use by 50–70% and length of stay by 50% compared to Finnegan scoring in multiple quality improvement studies. AAP endorses this approach.

If pharmacotherapy is needed:

  • First-line: Morphine — 0.05–0.1 mg/kg PO q3–4h PRN (titrate to ESC goals). Wean 10–20% every 24–48h as tolerated.
  • Alternative: Methadone — longer half-life; less frequent dosing (q8–12h). May allow faster weaning.
  • Adjunct: Clonidine — 0.5–1 µg/kg PO q4–6h (for autonomic symptoms). May reduce morphine duration.
  • Adjunct: Phenobarbital — for polysubstance exposure (non-opioid components) or refractory cases. NOT first-line for opioid-only withdrawal.

Non-pharmacologic interventions (ALWAYS first-line):

  • Rooming-in with mother (strongest intervention — reduces pharmacotherapy by 50%)
  • Breastfeeding (safe if mother is on MAT and HIV-negative; except if using illicit drugs)
  • Swaddling, low-light, low-noise environment
  • Skin-to-skin (kangaroo care)
  • Small frequent feeds, high-calorie formula (24 kcal/oz) if needed for weight gain
